title: Another person in Maine sickened by the rare Powassan virus - WMTW
snippet: # Another person in Maine sickened by the rare Powassan virus. The Maine Center for Disease Control says an adult in Lincoln County tested positive for the rare, and potentially deadly, Powassan virus last week. That is just the third case in Maine this year. The Maine CDC also said on Tuesday that a wild bird in Cumberland County tested positive for West Nile virus last week. That is the first positive case of West Nile virus in the state this year. Powassan is the only endemic arbovirus spread by ticks in Maine. Researchers at the vector-borne disease lab in Scarborough are studying Powassan and how ticks survive Maine's harsh winters. Powassan virus infection is a rare, but sometimes fatal, tick-borne disease and can spread from ticks to people in as little as 15 minutes after a bite from an infected deer or woodchuck tick. The CDC says cases of Powassan are rare in the United States, with only about 20 to 50 cases reported per year across the country from 2018 to 2023.

snippet: Residents across Florida and the Southeast face days of heavy rain and possible flooding as a tropical disturbance churns in the eastern Gulf, threatening dangerous conditions even if it does not develop into a named storm. title: West Nile virus found in Mecklenburg County mosquitoes: How to protect yourself - WBTV
snippet: # West Nile virus found in Mecklenburg County mosquitoes: How to protect yourself. (WBTV) - A mosquito sample collected in Mecklenburg County tested positive for West Nile virus, according to the county health department. The NC State Laboratory of Public Health tested a pool of mosquitos collected in Mecklenburg County on July 14. Those mosquitos tested positive for West Nile virus, the county health department reported on July 20. West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne illness and the number one cause of diseases spread by mosquitos in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or CDC. In early July, federal health officials reported that over 23 states have reported finding West Nile Virus -- the most in 10 years. There are no vaccines for humans and no medications to cure the West Nile virus once a person is infected by a mosquito, officials said.

title: Sloth Fever: Latin America's Oropouche Epidemic
snippet: Without global collaboration and action to address root causes, Oropouche fever is likely to continue spreading. Oropouche, a viral disease that has historically received little press coverage, is now emerging as a significant public health concern in Latin America. Traditionally confined to the Amazon Basin, the Oropouche virus has rapidly barreled through the region since a genetic mutation enhanced the virus's ability to spread in 2015. Experts are now sounding the alarm that Oropouche could soon become as common as diseases such as chikungunya, dengue, or Zika as deforestation, climate change, and urbanization accelerate the virus's rapid spread. It is sometimes known as sloth fever because scientists first detected the virus in sloths and believed that the animals had a significant role in its spread. Urbanization and deforestation can bring wildlife closer to human settlements, creating a suitable environment for reproducing midges that carry the Oropouche virus, reports a recent study.
